title: What should you ask first in an investment or capacity case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in an investment or capacity case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Should the client build a new plant, add capacity or make a big investment? Here is how to think it through.
body:
The first question to ask

Is demand real, and can existing capacity be squeezed?

How to build your structure

  • Need (is demand real and lasting, squeeze existing capacity first)
  • Economics (upfront and running cost, extra margin, payback, price effect if rivals add capacity)
  • Alternatives (outsource, lease, subcontract)
  • Execution (time to build, skills, risks)

The trap most people fall into

Approving capex before fixing bottlenecks.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the investment decision framework.

Two prompts to try

Should a UK university open a campus in Singapore?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Students in the region and their willingness to pay; Competition from local and other foreign universities
  • Economics: Set-up cost, fees, staff; Break-even student numbers
  • Quality and brand: Teaching and degrees equal to home; Risk to reputation
  • Regulation and partners: Local approvals; Partner or go alone

Where to start: Demand: will enough students pay close to UK fees in Singapore?

The trap: Assuming home demand carries over to a new market.

Should a delivery company switch its 2,000 vans to electric?

Show a model structure
  • Cost per mile: Van price, energy, maintenance; Resale value and grants
  • Operations: Range vs daily routes; Charging at depots, time to charge
  • Investment and timing: Upfront cost, financing; Switch all now vs as vans retire
  • Other benefits and risks: Clean-air zones, customer demands; Battery life, grid capacity

Where to start: Total cost per mile over a van's life, not the purchase price.

The trap: Comparing only purchase prices.
